problem: Existing LLM-based household navigation methods are single-agent and do not support communication and collaborative planning among multiple robots. Prior multi-agent LLM work is either centralized, which does not scale with team size, or uses fixed or importance-based leaders, which fail when tasks are equally important.
motivation: Searching for several objects in a household is hard and slow for one robot, so a team should divide the work. A team needs to decide what to communicate, whom to talk to, and how to plan globally after communicating. Leader-based communication is known to speed up consensus, and dynamic leadership helps further.
key_idea: Decentralized LLM agents describe rooms in language (GPT-4o) and pass a communication-triggered dynamic leadership, together with global information, from agent to agent. Each requesting agent asks the current leader, who resolves conflicts and assigns rooms and locked objects.
insight: The paper reports no experiments or ablations, so no evidence supports its claims. Its argument is that passing leadership to whoever last requested help spreads the communication load and keeps the team robust to a crashed robot, and that room-level descriptions give compact, task-relevant content for communication. These claims about consensus speed, fewer messages and conflict-freeness remain unverified.
method: Semantic map and topology: each robot builds a real-time local semantic map from RGB-D and pose, and extracts Voronoi waypoints and a topological map from the accessible-area channel.
Room description: rooms are segmented on the map. The robot rotates to capture 12 frames at each waypoint, picks the best frame per room, and GPT-4o generates a language description of it.

Comm-triggered dynamic leadership: the first agent to gather all room descriptions becomes the temporary leader. When agent b asks for help, the leader replies and passes on the global information, and b inherits the leadership.

Member proposal: the agent builds a prompt from its id, progress, states, shared goals, dialogue history and options. The LLM outputs a proposal with locked objects, a target room and thoughts (Ps_i = LLM(Pr(...))).

Leader coordination: the leader LLM takes the proposal plus global progress and states, checks conflicts, and returns a response for the requester (action, support or oppose, thoughts). It can also interrupt other agents and reassign their actions.
Motion planning: the robot selects the nearest Voronoi point in the target room, plans mid-term waypoints with Dijkstra on the topological graph, then uses Fast Marching Method for discrete actions.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen) for room description and LLM communication/planning
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D plus pose per robot, with 12-frame rotations at waypoints
setting.action_space: discrete actions from Fast Marching Method planning over topological waypoints
setting.simulator: not specified (the text describes no experimental setup)

numbers_note: The paper is a work-in-progress workshop version with no experiments, tables or results; it evaluates on the Sequence Agnostic MultiON task in name only.
results: No quantitative results are reported. The abstract only claims faster team consensus with fewer communications, and conflict-free, robust navigation as team size grows.
limitations: No experiments or quantitative evidence are provided, so all claims are unverified.
The mapping perception may fail on dynamic objects such as humans or pets, and the framework handles only single-floor navigation.
The system depends on GPT-4o and on sequential passing of leadership, whose cost and latency are not analyzed.
builds_on: Building Cooperative Embodied Agents Modularly with LLMs (CoELA)
Embodied LLM agents learn to cooperate in organized teams
compares_to: CoNav (Yu et al. 2023, centralized LLM navigation)
